name: CNS Tuberculosis (TB Meningitis)

pathogens.why: TB meningitis is caused by M. tuberculosis and is distinguished from bacterial meningitis by its subacute (days-to-weeks) evolution, basal meningeal involvement (often causing cranial nerve palsies and hydrocephalus), and characteristic CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, markedly elevated protein).

investigations.test: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis, AFB smear, CBNAAT/Xpert, and culture
investigations.why: CSF in TB meningitis classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, and high protein; CBNAAT provides faster confirmation and rifampicin resistance status than culture.
Identifies basal meningeal enhancement, tuberculomas, infarcts, and hydrocephalus — all characteristic complications requiring specific management.
Concurrent or prior pulmonary TB is common and supports the diagnosis.
TB meningitis is disproportionately seen in HIV co-infection, which changes overall management and prognosis.

references: National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) India Guidelines
reason: Subacute fever with neck stiffness, altered sensorium or focal deficits, evolving over days to weeks rather than hours (distinguishing it from acute bacterial meningitis), raises strong suspicion for tuberculous meningitis. Unlike pulmonary TB, empiric antitubercular therapy should be started promptly on strong clinical suspicion WITHOUT waiting for microbiological confirmation, since the morbidity and mortality of delayed treatment in TB meningitis is severe and confirmatory tests (culture) take weeks.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.1124, 1127, 1136, 1389; pharmacogenomics of adjunctive steroids p.1026
clinicalPearls: Typically evolves over 1-2 weeks (subacute) - a longer course than typical bacterial meningitis; often begins as headache plus subtle mental changes after a prodrome of weeks of low-grade fever, malaise, anorexia and irritability (p.1389).
Because meningeal involvement is most pronounced at the base of the brain, cranial nerve palsies (ocular nerves in particular) are a frequent finding (p.1389).
Involvement of cerebral arteries at the skull base can produce focal ischemia/infarction (p.1389).
Untreated, the disease progresses toward coma with hydrocephalus and intracranial hypertension (p.1389).
In more than half of cases, evidence of old pulmonary lesions or a miliary pattern is found on chest radiograph (p.1389).
CNS TB accounts for roughly 5% of extrapulmonary TB cases; it is seen most often in young children but also in adults, especially those with HIV (p.1389).

The last tube of CSF collected at lumbar puncture is the best tube to send for an AFB smear; if a pellicle or cobweb-like clot forms on the fluid surface, AFB are best demonstrated in a smear of that clot/pellicle (p.1127).
Empiric anti-tuberculous therapy is often started on a high index of clinical suspicion without adequate laboratory support, given the poor smear yield and slow culture (p.1127).

A lymphocytic pleocytosis with low CSF glucose should prompt consideration of fungal or tuberculous meningitis, Listeria meningoencephalitis, or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis (p.1124).
harrison.pathophysiology: Tuberculous meningitis in adults does not arise acutely from direct hematogenous seeding of the meninges. Rather, during hematogenous dissemination of primary infection, miliary (millet seed-sized) tubercles form in the brain parenchyma; these enlarge and usually caseate. Whether a caseous focus produces meningitis depends on its proximity to the subarachnoid space (SAS) and how quickly it becomes fibrous-encapsulated. Subependymal caseous foci discharge bacilli and mycobacterial antigens into the SAS; rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space is a recognized route. The mycobacterial antigens trigger an intense inflammatory reaction producing a thick exudate that fills the basilar cisterns and encases the cranial nerves and the major blood vessels at the base of the brain - explaining the basal enhancement, cranial nerve palsies, arteritic infarcts and obstructive hydrocephalus seen clinically. Meningitis can also result from hematogenous spread of primary or postprimary pulmonary TB, and is a particular concern in very young children and immunocompromised persons (e.g., people living with HIV) (p.1127, 1389).
additionalDifferentials: Fungal (subacute/chronic) meningitis, e.g. Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides immitis (p.1124, 1127)
infectionMimics: Cryptococcal meningitis (lymphocytic CSF with low glucose) (p.1124, 1127)
Viral meningitis due to mumps, LCMV, HSV-2, VZV or enteroviruses, which can occasionally cause low CSF glucose and mimic the TB profile (p.1124)
additionalInvestigations: CSF AFB smear taken from the last LP tube, or from any pellicle/cobweb clot - but smears are positive in only ~10-40% of adult cases (p.1127).
Mycobacterial CSF culture - gold standard, but takes 4-8 weeks and is positive in only ~50% to up to 80% of cases (p.1127, 1389).

CSF nucleic acid amplification testing - Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra or Xpert MTB/RIF; in the TB chapter the Xpert MTB/RIF assay has sensitivity up to 80% and is the preferred initial diagnostic option, with treatment started immediately on a positive result; a negative result does not exclude TB (p.1127, 1389).
Repeat lumbar puncture to increase diagnostic yield, since AFB are infrequently seen on a single direct smear (p.1389).

CT/MRI brain looking specifically for hydrocephalus and abnormal enhancement of the basal cisterns or ependyma; contrast-enhanced ring lesions on CT/MRI suggest tuberculoma (biopsy needed to confirm) (p.1389).
redFlags: Declining level of consciousness / progression toward coma (p.1389)
New cranial nerve palsies, especially ocular nerves, indicating basal meningeal involvement (p.1389)
Focal neurologic deficit suggesting arteritic cerebral infarction (p.1389)
Clinical or imaging evidence of hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure (p.1389)
Acute deterioration with severe headache, confusion, lethargy, altered sensorium and neck rigidity in a previously subacute presentation (p.1389)
harrison.prognosis: If unrecognized, tuberculous meningitis is uniformly fatal. The disease responds to chemotherapy, but neurologic sequelae are documented in about 25% of treated cases - most often when the diagnosis was delayed. Adjunctive glucocorticoids may speed resolution of CSF abnormalities and raised CSF pressure and lower rates of death or severe disability and relapse; in one trial adjunctive dexamethasone improved survival in patients >14 years but did not reduce the frequency of neurologic sequelae. Among people living with HIV, a placebo-controlled study showed no survival or secondary-endpoint benefit from a 6-8 week tapering course of adjunctive dexamethasone (p.1389). Pharmacogenomic data suggest only a subset of patients benefit from steroids: those homozygous for the proinflammatory LTA4H allele were most helped, whereas those homozygous for the anti-inflammatory allele may be harmed (p.1026).
pitfalls: Low CSF smear yield (AFB seen on direct smear in only ~10-40% of adult cases) and slow culture (4-8 weeks) mean diagnosis cannot wait for microbiologic confirmation - empiric anti-TB therapy is appropriately started on high clinical suspicion (p.1127).
Any one of the classic CSF parameters (cell count, protein, glucose) can be within the normal range, so a normal value does not exclude TB meningitis (p.1389).
A negative CSF Xpert MTB/RIF result does not exclude TB and requires further diagnostic workup (p.1389).
Early in the course CSF may show a neutrophil predominance rather than lymphocytes, which can mislead toward bacterial meningitis (p.1389).

Delayed recognition allows the subacute illness to evolve acutely (severe headache, confusion, altered sensorium, neck rigidity) and is the main driver of death and of the ~25% rate of neurologic sequelae (p.1389).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison describes a clinical continuum that maps to the British MRC staging used for TB meningitis: an early stage with headache and slight mental changes after a prodrome of low-grade fever/malaise/anorexia, evolving (if unrecognized) to severe headache, confusion, lethargy and altered sensorium with neck rigidity, and ultimately to coma with hydrocephalus and intracranial hypertension; outcome worsens markedly with more advanced stage at presentation/diagnostic delay (p.1389).
